answer: The history threat to internal validity arises when an external event occurs at the same time as a program and produces the change an evaluation might wrongly attribute to the program. In the tutorial's example, a county diabetes prevention program launches in January 2020 and emergency department visits drop 18%, but a statewide Medi-Cal expansion took effect the same month. A comparison county without the program improved 15%, leaving only a 3% difference, which suggests most of the apparent gain reflects the concurrent event rather than the program.

faqs.q: What is a concurrent event in a health program evaluation?
faqs.a: A concurrent event is something that changes at the same time as the program, such as an economic shift, another policy, or a seasonal factor. In the tutorial, the California Medi-Cal expansion of January 2020 affected all counties and improved access to preventive care everywhere.

faqs.q: How does a comparison group reveal a history threat?
faqs.a: A comparison group that did not receive the program but experienced the same outside events shows how much of the change was driven by those events. When the comparison county improved 15% versus the program county's 18%, only the 3% difference plausibly reflects the program.

faqs.q: Why can an 18% improvement still not prove a program worked?
faqs.a: Because if an outside event affected everyone, the observed drop blends the program effect with the event's effect. The tutorial shows that subtracting the comparison county's 15% improvement leaves a small difference that may be noise rather than a real program effect.
